findings.title: Async legacy writes derive from the request-scoped context, which is canceled once the handler returns
findings.body: In Create (and similarly in Delete line 110, Update line 135, and DeleteCollection line 163), the goroutine that performs the asynchronous Legacy write does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` using the `ctx` that was passed into the outer method, i.e. the request's context. The outer function returns immediately after the Storage write succeeds (it does not wait for the goroutine), so the HTTP handler completes and the underlying request context is typically canceled by the server right after the response is sent. Because the 10s timeout context is derived from (a child of) that request context, it will also be canceled as soon as the parent is canceled, aborting the legacy write before it has a chance to run or complete. This defeats the entire purpose of Mode 3's 'best effort' async legacy write, since legacy writes will routinely fail with context-canceled errors instead of actually persisting data. A decoupled context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh context carrying only the needed values) should be used as the parent for the goroutine's timeout context.

findings.title: Storage.Create failure incorrectly recorded as a legacy-storage duration metric
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. This mislabels a Unified Storage failure as a Legacy Storage failure in the metrics, corrupting the duration/error metrics used to monitor dual-write health. The same bug exists in `Update` (line 129) where a Storage.Update failure is also recorded via `recordLegacyDuration` instead of `recordStorageDuration`.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection result recorded using the Storage duration metric
findings.body: Inside the async goroutine of `DeleteCollection`, after calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. This mislabels the legacy-store outcome as a unified-storage outcome, corrupting dual-write metrics that are meant to distinguish storage vs legacy performance/error rates.

findings.title: Delete records object name instead of resource kind as a metric label
findings.body: In `Delete`, the successful-storage-delete metric call is `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the object's `name` (e.g. "foo") where every other call site in this file passes `options.Kind` (the resource kind, e.g. "playlists"). This introduces an unbounded, high-cardinality label value (one per deleted object name) into the metric instead of the intended bounded resource-kind label, which can blow up metric cardinality in Prometheus and also makes the recorded data inconsistent with the rest of the dual-writer metrics.

findings.title: Delete attaches the un-enriched logger to the context instead of the local contextual logger
findings.body: In `Delete`, `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` is built but then `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` attaches the base `d.Log` (without the name/kind/method values) to the context instead of the enriched `log`. Every other method in this file (Create, Get, List, Update, DeleteCollection) correctly propagates the enriched logger. As a result, any code downstream that pulls the logger via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` during a Delete call loses the name/kind/method structured fields, reducing log traceability specifically for deletes.

findings.title: Async legacy write failures are only recorded as metrics, never logged
findings.body: In the goroutines for Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the error returned from the Legacy store call (e.g. `errObjectSt` in Create) is only fed into `recordLegacyDuration`/`recordStorageDuration` as a boolean; it is never logged (e.g. via `log.Error(...)`). Previously (pre-PR) these failures were logged with contextual detail. Since these writes now happen asynchronously and their result is not surfaced to the caller at all, silently dropping the error message removes the only way an operator could discover/debug data divergence between Legacy and Unified storage, beyond a boolean metric increment.

findings.title: Mode3 tests never verify that the asynchronous legacy write actually occurs
findings.body: TestMode3_Create (and similarly TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_DeleteCollection) set up `m.On("Create"/"Delete"/"Update"/"DeleteCollection", ...)` expectations on the legacy mock, but since the real implementation now fires the legacy write in a goroutine, the test function can return before the goroutine executes. The tests never call `m.AssertExpectations(t)` / `m.AssertCalled(t, ...)` nor synchronize with the goroutine (e.g. via a channel/WaitGroup), so the test will pass whether or not the legacy write ever runs or succeeds. This leaves the core 'asynchronously write to legacy as a safety measure' behavior of Mode 3 effectively untested.
